paragraphs: The natural order of the subject now brings us to the provision of the Constitution that lets the national legislature regulate, in the last resort, the election of its own members. It reads: "The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the legislature thereof; but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators."(1) Those who condemn the Constitution wholesale have denounced this provision. So have those who object with less sweep and more moderation. And in one instance a gentleman who has declared himself the advocate of every other part of the system has found it objectionable.

Nevertheless, I am greatly mistaken if any article in the whole plan is more completely defensible. Its propriety rests on the evidence of one plain proposition: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION. Every just reasoner will approve, at first sight, of keeping to this rule in the work of the Convention. He will disapprove of every departure from it, unless it seems to have been forced by the need to include some particular ingredient that strict conformity with the rule would have ruled out. Even then he may accept the necessity, but he will still regard such a departure from so fundamental a principle as a portion of imperfection in the system, and regret it. It may prove the seed of future weakness, and perhaps of anarchy.

No one will claim that an election law could have been drafted and placed in the Constitution that would always fit every probable change in the country's situation. It will therefore not be denied that some discretionary power over elections must exist somewhere. I presume it will be as readily conceded that this power could reasonably have been arranged in only three ways. It had to be lodged wholly in the national legislature, or wholly in the State legislatures, or primarily in the latter and ultimately in the former. The Convention has, with reason, preferred the last. It has given the first regulation of elections for the federal government to the local administrations. In ordinary cases, and when no improper views prevail, they may be both more convenient and more satisfactory. But it has reserved to the national authority a right to step in whenever extraordinary circumstances might make this necessary for its safety.

Nothing is more evident than this: an exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy. They could destroy it at any moment by neglecting to provide for choosing the persons who administer its affairs. It does little good to say that such neglect or omission would be unlikely. The constitutional possibility of it, with nothing to balance the risk, is an unanswerable objection. Nor has any satisfactory reason yet been given for taking that risk. The extravagant surmises of a distempered jealousy can never be called a reason. If we are in the mood to presume abuses of power, it is as fair to presume them from the State governments as from the general government. Sound theory says it is more fitting to trust the Union with the care of its own existence than to hand that care to anyone else. So if we must risk abuses of power on one side or the other, it is more rational to risk them where the power would naturally be placed than where it would be placed unnaturally.

Suppose the Constitution had included an article empowering the United States to regulate elections for the individual States. Would anyone have hesitated to condemn it, both as an unwarranted transfer of power and as a deliberate engine for destroying the State governments? The violation of principle in that case would have needed no comment. To an unbiased observer it is just as plain in a scheme that makes the national government's existence, in a similar respect, depend on the pleasure of the State governments. An impartial look at the matter cannot fail to convince us that each government, as far as possible, ought to depend on itself for its own preservation.

Here is an objection to this position. The make-up of the national Senate, it may be said, would carry in its full extent the very danger that an exclusive power in the State legislatures to regulate federal elections is supposed to bring. By declining to appoint senators, the State legislatures might at any time strike a fatal blow at the Union. From this it may be inferred that since the Union's existence would thus depend on them in so essential a point, there can be no objection to trusting them with it in the particular case under consideration. It may be added that each State's interest in keeping its representation in the national councils would be a complete security against abuse of the trust.

This argument looks plausible, but it will not prove sound on examination. It is certainly true that the State legislatures, by refusing to appoint senators, may destroy the national government. It does not follow that because they hold such a power in one instance, they ought to hold it in every other. There are cases in which the harmful tendency of such a power may be far more decisive, and in which no motive as compelling as the one that must have guided the Convention in forming the Senate recommends admitting it. Insofar as that arrangement exposes the Union to possible injury from the State legislatures, it is an evil. But it was an evil that could not have been avoided without shutting the States, in their political capacities, entirely out of the organization of the national government. Had that been done, it would doubtless have been read as a complete abandonment of the federal principle. It would also certainly have deprived the State governments of the absolute safeguard they will enjoy under this provision. However wise it may have been to accept a drawback in this instance to gain a necessary advantage or a greater good, nothing follows from it in favor of piling up the evil where no necessity urges it and no greater good invites it.

We can also easily see that the national government would run a much greater risk from a State legislative power over the elections of its House of Representatives than from the State power to appoint members of its Senate. Senators are to be chosen for six years. A rotation will empty and refill the seats of a third of them every two years. No State is to have more than two senators, and a quorum of the body is to be sixteen members. Together, these circumstances mean that a temporary combination of a few States to suspend the appointment of senators could neither end the body's existence nor impair its activity. And a general and permanent combination of the States is not something we have anything to fear from. The first might come from sinister designs in the leading members of a few State legislatures. The last would require a fixed and rooted disaffection in the great body of the people. Either that will never exist at all, or it will in all probability come from experience of the general government's inability to advance their happiness, and in that event no good citizen could want it to continue.

The federal House of Representatives is different. A general election of its members is intended once every two years. Suppose the State legislatures were given an exclusive power to regulate these elections. Then every election time would be a delicate crisis in the national situation. It might end in the dissolution of the Union, if the leaders of a few of the most important States had conspired beforehand to prevent an election.

I do not deny that there is some weight in the observation that each State's interest in being represented in the federal councils will protect against abuse of a power over its elections held by the State legislatures. But those who note an obvious distinction will not think the protection complete. The people have an interest in the public happiness; their local rulers have an interest in the power and importance of their offices. The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union at times when the particular rulers of particular States may feel very differently. Those rulers are spurred by the natural rivalry of power and by hopes of personal aggrandizement, and each is supported by a strong faction in his State. This difference of feeling between a majority of the people and the individuals with the most credit in their councils is, in some of the States, visible at this very moment, on the present question. The scheme of separate confederacies, which will always multiply the chances of ambition, will be a never-failing bait to every influential character in the State administrations who is capable of preferring his own personal gain and advancement to the public welfare. Such men would hold a very effective weapon in the exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government. A combination of a few of them in a few of the most considerable States, where the temptation will always be strongest, might destroy the Union. They would only need to seize the opportunity of some casual dissatisfaction among the people (which perhaps they may themselves have stirred up) and stop choosing members for the federal House of Representatives. We should never forget that a firm union of this country under an effective government will probably be an increasing object of jealousy to more than one nation of Europe. Enterprises to subvert it will sometimes begin in the intrigues of foreign powers, and some of those powers will seldom fail to encourage and abet them. Wherever it can be avoided, then, its preservation ought not to be committed to the guardianship of anyone except those whose situation will always give them an immediate interest in the faithful and vigilant performance of the trust.
